regiones/gran-chaco/religiones.7.nota.texto: In the Northeast they went from 11.8% in 2008 to 23.1% in 2019 (CONICET surveys); it is the second most evangelical region in the country, after Patagonia. They are marked as important from 2019, the year of the survey that gives that figure; the survey's region does not exactly coincide with the Gran Chaco.

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Peoples of the Gran Chaco (Guaycurú, Mataco-Mataguayan and others)

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.1.nombre.texto: Chiriguanos (Ava Guaraní) and Chanés of the foothills

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.2.nombre.texto: Spanish and criollos of forts, reductions and estancias on the edge of the Chaco

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.5.nombre.texto: Creole, with European settlers (and Mennonites in the Paraguayan Chaco from 1927)

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.6.nombre.texto: Chaco peoples (Qom, Wichí, Pilagá, Mocoví, Nivaclé and others)

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.0.nota.texto: There are few archaeological studies of the Chaco before the conquest. From the 17th century, the peoples of the south adopted the horse.

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.5.nota.texto: The 2022 Argentine census counted 1,306,730 people (2.83%) who identify as Indigenous or as first-generation descendants, throughout the country; no figure was verified for the Gran Chaco as a whole.

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.6.nota.texto: Speakers of Chaco languages in Argentina: Wichí, about 27,000 (Pilcomayo variety, in Formosa) and about 32,000 (Chaco variety, in Chaco, Formosa and Salta); Qom, between 40,000 and 60,000 in 2006. In 2010 the province of Chaco declared Qom (Toba), Moqoit and Wichí co-official, alongside Spanish.

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.2.nombre.texto: Guaraní (Ava Guaraní; in the Paraguayan Chaco, also of the criollos)

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The distribution of languages before the 16th century is not known.

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Wichí: about 27,000 speakers of the Pilcomayo variety (Formosa) and about 32,000 of the Chaco variety (Chaco, Formosa and Salta); Nivaclé: about 200 in the northeast of Formosa (estimates cited in Wikipedia).

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.2.nota.texto: In Paraguay, Guaraní was spoken by 86% of the population in 2002 and by 77% in 2012 (censuses).

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.5.nota.texto: In 2010 the province of Chaco declared Qom, Moqoit and Wichí co-official, alongside Spanish.

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Qom: between 40,000 and 60,000 speakers in 2006; Mocoví (Moqoit): about 2,800 in 2012; Pilagá: between 2,000 and 5,000. Together the Guaicuruan languages have about 49,000 speakers in Argentina.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/resumen.texto: The region east of the Paraguay River, except Asunción and its surroundings (which go with the Río de la Plata): a land of forests and rivers inhabited by the Guaraní, where the Jesuits organized their reductions in the 17th and 18th centuries. Today it is home to Ciudad del Este and the Itaipú Dam.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.1.resume.texto: Asunción (1537) is the base of the Spanish colonization of the region.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.2.resume.texto: The Jesuits found Guaraní towns, such as Trinidad and Jesús, until their expulsion.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.3.resume.texto: Paraguay becomes independent in 1811 and is devastated by the War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870).

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.4.resume.texto: Stroessner's dictatorship (1954-1989) and the Itaipú Dam (1984).

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.4..texto: Protestantism (German colonists from 1887, Mennonites, Lutherans and evangelicals)

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.5..texto: Buddhism and other Asian religions (Japanese immigration)

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.0..texto: Before the arrival of the Spanish missionaries, the peoples of present-day Paraguay practiced a variety of religions.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.1..texto: Asunción, founded in 1537, had the first bishopric of the Río de la Plata, created by a papal bull of 1547; the first bishop, Friar Juan de los Barrios, was consecrated in 1548.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.2..texto: The 1609 cutoff is approximate: that year San Ignacio Guazú, the first Jesuit reduction in Paraguay, was founded, lying outside this region, and there is no figure that measures when Catholics became a majority. During the colonial period it was the only permitted religion. Today 88.2% are Catholic according to Vatican data cited on Wikipedia; the 2012 census counted 5,749,888 Catholics. Between 1996 and 2013 Catholicism lost almost 5 percentage points and evangelicals gained between 2 and 3.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.3..texto: The 2002 census includes a category for Indigenous religions.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.4..texto: It is the second affiliation, with 9.2% of the population (about 685,740 people). The date 1887 is that of the founding of the German colony of Nueva Germania (San Pedro, 23 August 1887), taken as an approximate starting point. The first Mennonite colony, Menno (1927), lies in the Chaco, outside this region; in the Región Oriental is Volendam, from 1947. Lutherans and Mennonites are the most traditional groups, and the most recent are evangelical and charismatic churches.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/religiones.5..texto: Japanese immigrants brought Buddhism. The Yguazú colony (Alto Paraná), founded on 22 August 1961, is the Japanese colony in this region with a known date; La Colmena (1936) and the Itapúa colonies lie outside the polygon.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.2.no.texto: Guaraní of the Jesuit reductions and of the Indian towns (pueblos de indios)

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.4.no.texto: Current Guaraní Indigenous peoples (Mbyá, Paĩ Tavyterá, Ñandeva and others)

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.0.no.texto: The first count of Indigenous people, in 1555, registered 100,000, and in 1611 some 800,000 “infidel Indians” were estimated in the Asunción area, a figure probably exaggerated, since the native population fell through wars, forced labor, forced relocations and disease. The Asunción area lies outside this region. The 1650 cutoff is approximate: there is no census that fixes it.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.1.no.texto: The first enslaved Africans arrived in 1556. According to historian José Ignacio Telesca, more than 4% of the population was enslaved in the colony; according to the association Kamba Cuá, in 1782 the Black population was 11.2% of the province's population. Current official estimates give around 2%.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.2.no.texto: The Río de la Plata reductions reached 141,182 inhabitants in 1732, in 30 missions spread across Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.3.no.texto: The 1650 cutoff is approximate and no source fixes it: no figure from that time was found. The available figures are later (141,182 inhabitants in the reductions in 1732, and between 96,000 and 97,480 in the province according to the viceregal census of 1778) and do not by themselves show a mestizo majority in 1650. The Paraguayan people originated in the massive union of Guaraní women with Spanish settlers in the 16th century; today it is estimated at 65% mestizo and 30% white.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.4.no.texto: The 2022 census counted 140,206 Indigenous people across the country (about 2.3%), including those of the Chaco. In 1848 President Carlos Antonio López granted citizenship to all of them, and many lost their names and their identity.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/culturas.5.no.texto: The Yguazú colony (Alto Paraná) was founded on 22 August 1961; La Colmena (1936) and the Itapúa colonies lie outside the polygon. In the 2002 census foreigners made up 3.4% of the population (81,592 Brazilians and 63,153 Argentines among the 173,176 foreigners).

regiones/paraguay-oriental/idiomas.0.not.texto: Guaraní was always more widely spoken than Spanish; it has been an official language alongside Spanish since 1992, and many non-Indigenous people use it too. 2012 census: 46.3% of households spoke Spanish and Guaraní (yopará), 34% only Guaraní and 15.3% only Spanish; use of Guaraní fell from 86% in 2002 to 77% in 2012. Permanent Household Survey (Encuesta Permanente de Hogares) of 2022: 34.3% are bilingual, 32.6% speak mostly Guaraní and 30.4% mostly Spanish.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/idiomas.1.not.texto: Spanish speakers were always a minority compared with Guaraní speakers; they were concentrated in the capital and among the classes with access to education.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/idiomas.2.not.texto: The 1870 cutoff, the year the War of the Triple Alliance ended, is approximate: no language census was found that fixes when Spanish became an important language. Close to 90% of the population speaks or understands it at least in part; it predominates in cities, education, the media and official documents.

regiones/amazonia-andina/resumen.texto: The forests and plains of eastern Peru and Bolivia: Loreto, Ucayali, Madre de Dios, Beni, Pando and Santa Cruz. Inhabited by Amazonian peoples such as the Asháninka, Shipibo and Mojeño, who built earthworks and raised fields in the Llanos de Mojos, it was a mission frontier and, c. 1900, the scene of the rubber boom.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.0.resumen.texto: Societies of the forest and the Llanos de Mojos, with earthworks and raised fields.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Jesuits found the missions of Mojos (1682) and Chiquitos.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.2.resumen.texto: After independence, Peru and Bolivia barely control the region.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.3.resumen.texto: Iquitos and Riberalta grow with rubber; abuses against Indigenous peoples, as in the Putumayo.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.4.resumen.texto: Colonization, oil, gas and agricultural expansion in Santa Cruz.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/resumen.texto: The valleys, puna and sierras of northwestern Argentina and the Cuyo region: Jujuy, Salta, Tucumán, Catamarca, La Rioja, San Juan, Mendoza and San Luis. Land of the Diaguita, Omaguaca, Atacama and Huarpe and of cultures such as La Aguada, it was the southeastern edge of Tawantinsuyu and the colonial route between Upper Peru and the Río de la Plata.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.0.resum.texto: The Condorhuasi, Aguada and Santa María cultures; Diaguita, Omaguaca and Huarpe.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.1.resum.texto: The Inca Empire incorporates the northwest and northern Cuyo into Collasuyu.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.2.resum.texto: Founding of Santiago del Estero (1553), Mendoza (1561), Tucumán (1565), Salta (1582) and Jujuy (1593), and the Calchaquí Wars.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.3.resum.texto: A front in the War of Independence (Güemes) and, later, Argentine provinces of sugar and wine.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.1.texto: Andean religion (hills, huacas and ancestors; Inca sun worship from the late 15th century)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.0.texto: Known only from rock art and burials.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.1.texto: Capacocha offerings on summits such as Llullaillaco show the religion of the Inca state.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.3.texto: According to the CONICET national survey (Wikipedia, “Religion in Argentina”), Catholics in the Northwest fell from 91.7% in 2008 to 76.0% in 2019, and those in Cuyo from 82.6% to 69.6%.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.4.texto: Syncretic practices, strong in the puna and the valleys. Worship of Pachamama remains widespread in Salta and Jujuy alongside Catholic beliefs, without opposition from the bishops.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.5.texto: Almost 4% in the Northwest and 10% in Cuyo in 2008, according to the CONICET survey. They are marked as a minority up to 2018: the cutoff is approximate, because there are only surveys from 2008 and 2019.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.6.texto: From 1.8% in 2008 to 5.0% in 2019 (CONICET); it remains the region with the fewest people with no religion in the country.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.7.texto: In 2019, according to the CONICET survey, 16.7% in the Northwest and 14.5% in Cuyo. They are marked as significant from 2019, the year of the survey that gives these figures; before that there is only the 2008 survey.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.0.n.texto: Hunter-gatherers of the puna and the valleys

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.1.n.texto: Andean farmers and herders of the Northwest (Tafí, Condorhuasi, Ciénaga, La Aguada, Santa María, Belén) and Huarpes in Cuyo

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.2.n.texto: Andean peoples under Inca rule (Diaguitas, Omaguacas, Atacamas, Huarpes)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.3.n.texto: Diaguitas, Calchaquíes, Omaguacas, Atacamas and Huarpes, under encomienda or at war

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.4.n.texto: Spanish, criollos and mestizos of the cities (Tucumán, Mendoza, San Juan, Salta, La Rioja, Jujuy, Catamarca)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.0.n.texto: Occupations such as that of Inca Cueva, about 10,000 years old. The domestication of the llama and the first crops led to herding and agriculture.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.2.n.texto: Chronicles date the Inca conquest to around 1471–1493; archaeological dates suggest it began a few decades earlier.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.3.n.texto: The Calchaquí valleys resisted until 1667; afterward many peoples were deported to other cities.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.5.n.texto: From 1880, with Spanish, Italian and Syrian-Lebanese immigration, mainly in Cuyo and Tucumán.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.6.n.texto: Majority in the puna and the Quebrada de Humahuaca. The Kollas are a group into which much of the Atacama, Omaguaca, Calchaquí and Chicha peoples merged, with a strong Quechua influence. Some of the Aymara and Quechua people in the area are recent immigrants from Bolivia and Peru (since the last decades of the 20th century). Across the country, the 2022 census counted 1,306,730 people (2.83%) who identify as Indigenous.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.0.no.texto: Indigenous languages of the Northwest and Cuyo (Kakán, Kunza, Huarpe and others)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.1.no.texto: Kakán, Kunza, Huarpe and other local languages

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.2.no.texto: Quechua, the general language of the Tawantinsuyu and of evangelization

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.0.no.texto: There is no record of the languages spoken before the conquest; those known were written down in the colonial period.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.1.no.texto: Kakán died out toward the late 17th century without leaving texts. Of the Huarpe languages, there remain the works of Luis de Valdivia (1607).

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.5.no.texto: South Bolivian Quechua is spoken in the puna and in Jujuy, Salta and Tucumán (about 5,100 speakers in 2004, according to an estimate cited on Wikipedia). Santiago del Estero Quechua, a different variety spoken in Santiago del Estero, outside this region, is not counted.

regiones/patagonia/resumen.texto: The plateaus and the Patagonian Andes south of the Colorado River, down to Tierra del Fuego. Inhabited by the Tehuelche, Mapuche, Selk'nam and Yaghan, it was explored by Magellan in 1520 and occupied by the Argentine state in the so-called Conquest of the Desert (1878-1885). Chilean Patagonia goes with Chile, and the Falkland Islands (Malvinas) fall outside the polygon.

regiones/patagonia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Guanaco hunters and canoe peoples of the Fuegian channels; the paintings of the Cueva de las Manos are more than 9,000 years old.

regiones/patagonia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Magellan, Darwin and the Welsh of Chubut (1865); Patagonia remains in Indigenous hands.

regiones/patagonia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Conquest of the Desert, extermination of the Selk'nam, national territories and later provinces; oil in Comodoro Rivadavia (1907).

regiones/patagonia/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Religions of the Patagonian and Fuegian peoples

regiones/patagonia/religiones.3.nombre.texto: Protestantism (Welsh settlers of Chubut, Anglican mission in Ushuaia)

regiones/patagonia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Among them, the initiation ceremonies of the selk'nam (Hain) and Yaghans that Gusinde recorded.

regiones/patagonia/religiones.4.nota.texto: It is the least Catholic region in the country: from 61.5% in 2008 to 51.0% in 2019, according to the CONICET national survey.

regiones/patagonia/religiones.5.nota.texto: In 2004 the Mapuche population in Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz was estimated at about 110,000 people; the 2022 census counted 1,306,730 people (2.83%) who identify as Indigenous across the country.

regiones/patagonia/religiones.6.nota.texto: It is the region with the most evangelicals in the country: 21.6% in 2008 and 24.4% in 2019 (CONICET surveys).

regiones/patagonia/religiones.7.nota.texto: From 11.7% in 2008 to 24.3% in 2019 (CONICET): after Greater Buenos Aires, it is the region with the most people with no religion.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Nomadic hunters of Patagonia (ancestors of the Tehuelches and Gününa Küna; horse riders from the 18th century)

regiones/patagonia/culturas.2.nombre.texto: Mapuche of northern Patagonia (Pehuenches, País de las Manzanas)

regiones/patagonia/culturas.3.nombre.texto: Criollos of Carmen de Patagones and the coastal forts

regiones/patagonia/culturas.5.nombre.texto: Criollo, with Chilean and European immigrants

regiones/patagonia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Occupations dating back about 13,000 years at Piedra Museo and Los Toldos.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.1.nota.texto: Predominant in Tierra del Fuego until the massacres and epidemics of 1880–1920.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.2.nota.texto: The eastward spread of the Mapuche, called araucanización, is documented; its interpretation is debated.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Welsh colony founded in 1865 in the lower valley of the Chubut River.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.6.nota.texto: In 2004 the Mapuche population in Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz was estimated at about 110,000 people.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.7.nota.texto: Southern Tehuelche (aonek'o 'a'jen) had barely two hundred speakers in the 1966 census, in Santa Cruz, and one source considers it extinct as of 2019.

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.4.nombre.texto: Mapudungun, widely used in northern Patagonia

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The languages of the first inhabitants are not known; the Chon languages are those recorded since the 16th century.

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Its spread among the peoples of northern Patagonia is part of the so-called Araucanization.

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.6.nota.texto: About 25,000 people spoke it as a second language in 1998; an estimate from 2008 puts it at around 5,000, and another from 2017 says there are no more than 5,000.

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.8.nota.texto: About 8,400 speakers in 2004 in Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz, with an ethnic population of about 110,000 people.

regiones/chile/resumen.texto: The long strip between the Andes and the Pacific, from the Atacama Desert to Tierra del Fuego. Inhabited by the Chinchorro, Atacameño, Diaguita, Mapuche and the peoples of the channels, its north was part of Tawantinsuyu; the Mapuche halted the Spanish conquest at the Biobío and kept Araucanía independent until the Chilean occupation of 1861-1883, and Chile became independent in 1818.

regiones/chile/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Chinchorro culture mummifies its dead from c. 5000 BC; Atacameño, Diaguita and Mapuche.

regiones/chile/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Incas reach the Maule River.

regiones/chile/eras.2.resumen.texto: Valdivia founds Santiago (1541); the Arauco War halts the Spanish at the Biobío.

regiones/chile/eras.3.resumen.texto: Independence (1818), the War of the Pacific against Peru and Bolivia (1879-1883) and the occupation of Araucanía.

regiones/chile/eras.4.resumen.texto: Saltpeter and copper; Pinochet's dictatorship (1973-1990) and democracy.

regiones/chile/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Indigenous religions (Mapuche, Aymara, Atacameño, Diaguita and those of the southern peoples)

regiones/chile/religiones.3.nombre.texto: Mapuche religion (machis and longkos, in independent Araucanía)

regiones/chile/religiones.0.nota.texto: This layer begins at -7000, the start of the region's first era; there is no record of the religions of that time. For the Mapuche, the machis were the main spiritual authorities, called by Ngenechén, the “Supreme Being”; the Aymara had a polytheistic religion tied to nature (Mallku, the achachilas, the Pachamama). José Bengoa estimates between 705,000 and 900,000 Mapuche between the Itata and the Reloncaví sound in the mid-16th century (Wikipedia, “Mapuche”), and after Curalaba (1598) the area south of the Biobío, except Chiloé, remained independent until 1861–1883. Colonial censuses counted about 79% white population around 1810, although current estimates range from under 20% to over 60%: the 1810 cutoff is approximate, because it is the first figure for the whole.

regiones/chile/religiones.1.nota.texto: The north was part of the Tawantinsuyu between 1470 and 1541.

regiones/chile/religiones.2.nota.texto: Catholic evangelization began with the conquistadors, because it was the only official religion of the Spanish Empire; the first Christian church, the church of San Francisco in Chiu Chiu, dates from the 1540s.

regiones/chile/religiones.3.nota.texto: The Mapuche halted the Spanish conquest at the Biobío and kept an independent Araucanía until the Chilean occupation of 1861–1883.

regiones/chile/religiones.4.nota.texto: It was the official religion until 1925, when the Constitution separated Church and State. The 2024 census counted 53.7% Catholics (aged over 15), 25.7% with no religion, 16.2% Protestants and 3.8% of other religions; in the 2002 census, 65% of Indigenous people were Catholic, 29% evangelical and 6% of other religions.

regiones/chile/religiones.5.nota.texto: Protestants arrived in the first half of the 19th century: the American missionary David Trumbull arrived in 1845 (the first Anglican church, in Valparaíso, dates from 1848); the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal was founded on 12 September 1909.

regiones/chile/religiones.6.nota.texto: Mapuche communities, 87% of Indigenous citizens, still respect the traditional religious leaders (longkos and machis), with a high degree of syncretism.

regiones/chile/religiones.7.nota.texto: The 2024 census counted 2,466,607 evangelicals (16.2%); Latinobarómetro in 2017 put them at 11%, and the Encuesta Nacional Bicentenario at 30%. The surveys disagree because of how the question is asked.

regiones/chile/religiones.8.nota.texto: The 2019 Encuesta Nacional Bicentenario gave 32% with no religion. The figures differ widely: 25.7% in the 2024 census (aged over 15), nearly 40% with no affiliation in the AmericasBarometer survey of 2023, and 10% non-religious in a 2022 estimate. There is no comparable series.

regiones/chile/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Indigenous peoples (Mapuche, Atacameños, Diaguitas, Aymara, Changos and canal peoples)

regiones/chile/culturas.7.nombre.texto: German and other immigration (Croats, British, Arabs)

regiones/chile/culturas.0.nota.texto: This layer begins at -7000, the start of the region's first era. José Bengoa estimates between 705,000 and 900,000 Mapuche between the Itata and the Reloncaví sound in the mid-16th century (Wikipedia, “Mapuche”), and after Curalaba (1598) the area south of the Biobío, except Chiloé, remained independent until 1861–1883. Colonial censuses counted about 79% white population around 1810, although current estimates range from under 20% to over 60%: the 1810 cutoff is approximate, because it is the first figure for the whole. Today there are about fifteen Indigenous languages, all isolates or from small families.

regiones/chile/culturas.2.nota.texto: The first enslaved Africans arrived in 1536 with Almagro's expedition. There were no large plantations, and captured Mapuche labor was cheaper; it is estimated that some 6,000 Africans were taken directly to Chile. The 1811 free-womb law halted slavery. Arica had a considerable Afro-descendant population in the colonial period.

regiones/chile/culturas.4.nota.texto: The Mapuche halted the conquest at the Biobío, and Araucanía remained independent until the Chilean occupation of 1861–1883.

regiones/chile/culturas.5.nota.texto: There are no censuses for this span; most figures are dated to 1810, using the colonial censuses (see the next entry).

regiones/chile/culturas.6.nota.texto: Colonial censuses counted about 79% white population in 1810, but current estimates range from under 20% to over 60%; the genetic study by the University of Brasília found 51.6% European ancestry, 42.1% Amerindian and 6.3% African.

regiones/chile/culturas.7.nota.texto: Between 1846 and 1914 some 30,000 Germans arrived, and the government promoted German immigration in 1848 to colonize the south. An estimated 380,000 are descendants of Croats (2.4%), more than 700,000 have British ancestry (4.5%), and some 800,000 are descendants of immigrants from Asia, mainly Palestinians, Syrians and Lebanese (5%). The 1907 census recorded the highest percentage of Europeans (2.2%); Chile was never an attractive destination for European immigration.

regiones/chile/culturas.8.nota.texto: The 2002 census, which counted only those who practiced an Indigenous culture or spoke an Indigenous language, gave 4.6% (692,192 people), of whom 87.3% declared themselves Mapuche; in the 2011 Latinobarómetro, 8% identified as Indigenous.

regiones/chile/idiomas.0.nombre.texto: Indigenous languages (Mapudungun, Cacán, Kunza, Aymara and others)

regiones/chile/idiomas.6.nombre.texto: Aymara, Quechua, Rapa Nui, Kawésqar and other current Indigenous languages

regiones/chile/idiomas.0.nota.texto: This layer begins at -7000, the start of the region's first era. There are about fifteen varieties that could be considered distinct languages and, unlike other South American countries, no large family: all are isolates or belong to families of three or four languages. José Bengoa estimates between 705,000 and 900,000 Mapuche between the Itata and the Reloncaví sound in the mid-16th century (Wikipedia, “Mapuche”), and after Curalaba (1598) the area south of the Biobío, except Chiloé, remained independent until 1861–1883. Colonial censuses counted about 79% white population around 1810, although current estimates range from under 20% to over 60%: the 1810 cutoff is approximate, because it is the first figure for the whole.

regiones/chile/idiomas.4.nota.texto: There are no language censuses for this span; most figures are dated to 1810, using the colonial censuses (see the next entry).

regiones/chile/idiomas.5.nota.texto: It is spoken by 99.3% of the population, in Chilean Spanish and, to a lesser extent, in its Andean and Chilote forms.

regiones/chile/idiomas.6.nota.texto: 2024 census: Aymara, 60,605 speakers; Chilean Quechua, 39,430; Rapa Nui, 7,006; Kawésqar, 656; Kunza, about 2,616, in revival.

regiones/chile/idiomas.7.nota.texto: It is spoken in rural enclaves in the south and as a second language in communities in larger cities.

regiones/chile/idiomas.8.nota.texto: 381,762 people, with varying levels of proficiency, spoke it in the 2024 census (the 2002 estimate was 100,000 to 200,000), mainly in Biobío, Araucanía, the Metropolitan Region and Los Ríos.

regiones/australia/resumen.texto: The Australian continent and Tasmania. Aboriginal peoples have lived there for at least 50,000 years, with one of the oldest continuous cultural traditions in the world; Great Britain founded a penal colony in Sydney in 1788, and in 1901 the colonies federated into the Commonwealth of Australia.

regiones/australia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hundreds of peoples and languages, with rock art and millennia-old oral traditions; contacts with Macassan fishermen in the north.

regiones/australia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Penal and free colonies, the gold rush (1851) and the dispossession and massacres of Aboriginal peoples.

regiones/australia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Federation in 1901; the 1967 referendum includes Aboriginal people in the national census.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/resumen.texto: The North and South Islands, one of the last great landmasses settled by humans: the Polynesian ancestors of the Māori arrived c. 1250–1300. After the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) it was a British colony, and in 1907 it became a self-governing dominion; in 1893 it was the first country to give women the vote.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.0.resumen.texto: Polynesians arrive c. 1250–1300 and develop Māori culture.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.1.resumen.texto: Cook charts the islands; whalers and missionaries arrive, and the Musket Wars break out.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.2.resumen.texto: Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and the New Zealand Wars over Māori land.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.3.resumen.texto: Dominion from 1907 and fully sovereign from 1947.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/demografia.0.nota.texto: New Zealand. Polynesians arrived c. 1250–1300: earlier values from the HYDE model are not shown.

regiones/melanesia/resumen.texto: Eastern New Guinea (Papua New Guinea), the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji (the Indonesian half of New Guinea belongs to Maritime Southeast Asia). Agriculture was invented independently in the New Guinea Highlands between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago, and from about 3,000 years ago the seafarers of the Lapita culture spread through these islands on their way to Polynesia.

regiones/melanesia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Settlers who arrived more than 40,000 years ago; early agriculture at Kuk.

regiones/melanesia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Lapita culture (c. 1600–500 BC) brings pottery and open-ocean navigation to the islands.

regiones/melanesia/eras.2.resumen.texto: European explorers from the 16th century; British, German, French and Australian colonies, and forced recruitment of laborers for Queensland and Fiji.

regiones/melanesia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), the Solomon Islands (1978) and Vanuatu (1980); New Caledonia remains French.

regiones/melanesia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji.

regiones/micronesia/resumen.texto: Thousands of small islands and atolls north of Melanesia: Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marianas, the Marshall Islands, Nauru and Kiribati. The Marianas were settled by Austronesian seafarers about 3,500 years ago; the islands were a stopover for the Spanish galleons, a German and Japanese colony, and the scene of battles and nuclear tests in the 20th century.

regiones/micronesia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Settlement of the Marianas (c. 1500 BC) and then the rest; Nan Madol, on Pohnpei, is the capital of the Saudeleur.

regiones/micronesia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Magellan reaches Guam (1521), and Spain colonizes the Marianas from 1668.

regiones/micronesia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Germany buys the islands from Spain (1899) and Japan occupies them from 1914; battles of the Second World War.

regiones/micronesia/eras.3.resumen.texto: UN trust territory under the United States, nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak (1946–1958), and independence beginning with Nauru (1968).

regiones/micronesia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Federated States of Micronesia, Palau, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, Marshall Islands, Nauru and Kiribati.

regiones/polinesia/resumen.texto: The great triangle of islands of the central and eastern Pacific: Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna, Niue, Tokelau and Pitcairn. Its navigators, guided by the stars, the swells and the birds, settled these islands between c. 900 BC and 1300; Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island, also Polynesian, lie outside this polygon.

regiones/polinesia/eras.0.resumen.texto: From Tonga and Samoa the Polynesians reach the Society Islands and the Marquesas, and from there Hawaii, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.

regiones/polinesia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Tongan empire, the marae of Tahiti and societies of hereditary chiefs.

regiones/polinesia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Wallis reaches Tahiti (1767); Cook, the mutiny on the Bounty (1789) and the missionaries; France annexes Tahiti (1880).

regiones/polinesia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Samoa (1962) and Tonga (1970) become independent; France conducts nuclear tests at Mururoa (1966–1996).

regiones/polinesia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Samoa, American Samoa, Tonga, Niue, Wallis and Futuna, Tokelau, Cook Islands, French Polynesia and Tuvalu.
